idiom_name: property access and destructuring with defaults (no binding layer exists)
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no payload binding to opt out of: JSON.parse yields plain objects, so the reader is simply the function that destructures the fields it needs and the language makes everything else inert. Destructuring defaults (const { total = 0 } = node) supply the missing-field half, and because no schema is consulted, a producer's new field can never break the reader. When validation is genuinely required at the boundary, add it explicitly (zod, ajv) - note that zod's object schemas strip unrecognised keys by default, which preserves the tolerant behaviour, while .strict() is the deliberate opt-in to reject them.
pitfalls: A destructuring default applies only when the value is undefined: an explicit null (or "", 0) passes through untouched, so `?? fallback` is needed when null must also mean absent.
Deep reads on optional branches throw: payload?.a?.b with fallbacks (or a helper) is required, because there is no schema to create missing intermediate objects.

Copying payloads wholesale (Object.assign, spread into a domain object, a JSON.parse reviver, unchecked __proto__/constructor keys) re-imports the coupling and can smuggle prototype pollution - read fields explicitly instead.
